p: On the April drill Saturday, once two two eight was in the air, Kit shut Boyd's office door and told him herself. Her Pilot score in 2019 had been nineteen. She'd said yes to his inspection so she'd never have to say nineteen on that ramp, and she'd let him pay on it ever since.

Boyd was relieved and angry at once. Every time a board went up, he said, he'd looked at her and thought, there's the one I cost. Then he gave her his own reason for sitting on her slip. When the old jets go, he goes, and he'd built her to stay. Her name on every launch had been both, keeping her close and showing her to the colonel. She told him she was sorry he'd carried it, and that she still wanted to go.

At lunch in the heritage room, Vern took the old attitude indicator out of its case and drew a live one on the slate: the little airplane stays put, the horizon moves, and the higher end of the horizon line is the low wing. Then he held up a model tanker, nose toward her, the way the test's pictures are drawn. She asked him whether he'd been on family day in 2001. He said there'd been one that June, and that its log was the one he hadn't picked.

That afternoon, chocked in the left seat for an engine run, she read the panel the way a pilot would for the first time. Sunday at noon Vern gave her the log from June 9, 2001. Two two eight on static display, a girl about seven who wouldn't get out of the navigator's seat, and a hole in the ceiling where the stars come in. The girl had asked which seat was the best one. He'd told her this one, and she hadn't believed him. He asked Kit if it was her. She said she didn't know yet, and she'd call him from her mother's.

Before release Boyd read her a letter of recommendation he'd written in pencil at his kitchen table, and made her look at him while he read it. It ended, seven years ago I asked her to stay, and she did. I am not asking again. He told her that her name stays under the window until she flies it.

At her mother's table across the river, over a roast, Kit told Rhonda about 2019. Then she lifted April's lunch menu off the family day picture on the freezer door. A man's hand pointed at a small round fitting in the ceiling, and the ring on it was Vern's. Rhonda said Kit had cried from the gate to the bridge that day, because she wanted to go back and sit in it. Kit asked if she could have the picture, and Rhonda said it had been hers since she was seven. On the phone that night, Vern said, you didn't believe me. No, sir, she said. Keep it that way, Sergeant.

I want to fly, at the bottom of the page, where the line about giving back to the wing used to be. Kit read it once, all the way to the period, at ten to seven on a Monday. Graham's truck was gone already. The house had its school day quiet, the dishwasher done, the furnace still making up its mind. LETTER 2, on the laptop at the kitchen table, next to a cold piece of toast. She'd typed it on a Saturday night in February and couldn't make herself hit Print. Now she did.
The printer was in the spare room, and she got there before the furnace kicked on and gave her something else to listen to. Copies, 1.

The page came out warm on top of Graham's box of old lab manuals. She put it in the folder with Boyd's pencil letter. Then she dragged LETTER to the trash and emptied it. The laptop made its little crumpling noise. She'd never noticed it was that loud.
Graham had stuck a yellow note on the coffee maker, over the switch, the same spot she'd used Friday. His printing, which was better than hers. One word.
The stars never waited on me, Sergeant. I got them in the same order every night, or I didn't get them.

After the break, the long inventory and Physical Science, three blocks come back to back, and all three are built for speed. Table Reading is ninth. Instrument Comprehension is tenth, and you had that one in April. Block Counting comes eleventh. The current Pearson page gives it 30 questions in 5 minutes. The 2015 pamphlet said 4.5 minutes for the same thirty, so check your own notice. Call it ten seconds a question on the new clock, nine on the old one, and nobody finishes it by staring.

Block Counting shows you a drawing of a pile of blocks, all the same size and shape, stacked on a table. A few of them carry numbers. Each question names one numbered block and asks how many other blocks it touches. Five choices, all of them counts. A pile serves several questions, so one drawing does a run of them, and on our practice tests that's six piles, five questions per pile. Pilot doesn't use this block. The navigator's composite does, on both lists I've seen, and I take that a little personally.
How the exam asks it. Thirty questions, five minutes, about ten seconds each, several per pile.

Here's the whole rule, and I want you to say it back to me. A block touches another block when they meet face to face, one flat side against another flat side. It doesn't have to be the whole face. A block lying across two others touches both of them, even if it only covers half of each, and a partial face counts. Edges and corners don't count. Two blocks that meet only along a line, or at a point, aren't touching on this test. And the table doesn't count. It's furniture.
Pile A. Pile A. A pile of 8 blocks, 4 on the bottom, 3 in layer 2, 1 in layer 3. Numbered blocks: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

Look at numbered block 2 in Pile A. It lies in the second layer, toward the back, half on one block and half on another, and one of those two you can't see. We'll get to that. Out front, in its own layer, blocks 3 and 4 each share part of a long face with it, so you're up to four, and block 1 lying crossways on top makes five. Behind it there's nothing, and nothing at either end. Five blocks touch it face to face, and not one of them shows you its whole face against block 2.

I learned that rule off a loadmaster at Mather in 1974, with a grease pencil and a pallet of crates. Every crate that leaned flat on another one got a check mark. The ones that only kissed at a corner didn't. He said those weren't holding anything up, and he was right, and he made me carry the crates anyway.
How the exam asks it. Count shared faces, whole or partial. Not an edge, not a corner, not the table.
Pile B. Pile B. A pile of 5 blocks, 3 on the bottom, 2 in layer 2. Numbered blocks: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

Block 4 in Pile B sits off by itself on the table, out front. Its back corner meets the corner of block 3 along one up and down line, the way two dominoes do when somebody sets them down crooked. That's an edge, and blocks that touch edges only aren't touching. So block 4 touches nothing at all, and here zero is the honest count. Plenty of people would put one, because they can see the two blocks meeting. Meeting isn't touching, not on this subtest.

Now block 1, lying crossways on top. It sits across blocks 5 and 3, half on each. Two. Block 2 lies right beside it, long side against long side. Three. Block 1 never gets near block 4. Three's the count. The other place corners hide is up a layer and over one. A block on top and a block on the table beside the pile can meet along a single line where the top one's bottom edge runs along the lower one's top edge. That's a line too. No face, no count.
How the exam asks it. Two blocks that meet on a line or at a point aren't touching. Look twice at anything diagonal.

At the nav table a star fix was three stars, shot through the port in the ceiling, worked on paper and plotted. I shot them in the same order every night. Same stars when I could get them, same sequence down the sheet, same pencil. Not because I was superstitious. When the order never changed, I never had to think about the order, and I could spend all of me on the star.

This subtest wants the same thing. Pick an order and never change it. Mine goes top, then bottom, then around the sides the same way round every time, back and right end and front and left end. That's how I walked a jet with a flashlight before a night sortie, and it's how you walk two two eight now without thinking about it. Count under your breath as you go. When you get back to where you started you've got your number, and you didn't count anybody twice or leave anybody out.

That's a systematic count, and it's the one habit that makes Block Counting go. I had a boom operator in 1983, Dale, who called receivers off the left wing first, every time, even when there was only the one out there. The pilots teased him about it for a year. He never lost one, and they never did figure out that was the reason. Without an order your eye jumps to whatever looks biggest in the drawing and wanders off from there. With one, a block boxed in on five sides takes about as long as a block with one neighbor.
How the exam asks it. Top, bottom, then around the sides, the same way round on every block. The order does the remembering.

The drawing is a 3D pile seen from up high and off one corner, about the way the tower sees a stack of pallets on the ramp. So some blocks sit behind others, or under them, and you never see a face of them. You count them anyway. Hidden blocks. The first one I ever met was a crate on a load diagram, buried under two others, and I left it off and would've bet a paycheck I was right. You find them with the oldest rule in a hangar, which is that nothing floats. The loadmaster who caught me just pointed at the crate on top and asked me what it was sitting on, air? I said no, sir. He said then go find out what. In these piles the what is always another block, the same size as the rest.
Pile C. Pile C. A pile of 6 blocks, 3 on the bottom, 3 in layer 2. Numbered blocks: 1, 2.

Look at block 1 in Pile C, front of the top layer. Under it lie two blocks crossways on the table, and all you get of them is two little square ends down the front, like two by fours poking out of a lumber rack. That's plenty. Behind it lies a plain block you only ever see the top of, long side against long side. Block 2, crossways, butts up against its right end. Four in all, and not one of them shows you the face it shares with block 1. I'd sign for every one.

The seams help too. Those two square ends tell you the bottom row runs crossways, front to back, under the whole thing. A line across the top of a layer is where one block quits and the next begins, and the rows you can't see are usually laid like the ones you can. Sometimes you honestly can't tell. Then quit squinting and ask what's holding up what you can see, all the way down to the table. Nine times in ten that's your hidden block. Patrice does a thousand piece puzzle every winter on the card table in the den, humming Glenn Miller at it, and I've learned to stay out of there. She finds the missing piece by staring at the hole, not the box.
How the exam asks it. Ask what the top blocks are sitting on. Air isn't an answer. Count whatever is.

Each pile serves a run of questions, one per numbered block. You know two two eight by her drips. After a year on a jet a crew chief can walk up to it in the dark and tell you which panel somebody's had open. A pile is the same, only it takes ten seconds instead of a year. So spend your first look at a new pile learning its shape, not just the block they asked about. How many layers. Which way each layer runs. Where the gaps are. Where there have to be hidden blocks. By the third question on it you aren't reading a drawing anymore. You're reading a pile you know.

Here's the whole run on Pile A, the way I'd do it with a pencil in my teeth. Block 1 lies crossways on top, resting on 2 and 3, and that's its whole list, two. Block 2 you already did, five. Block 3 sits up front in the second layer on the block under it, with 2 at its back and 4 against its right end, and it carries part of 1, so it comes to four. Block 4 rides on 5, with 2 behind it and 3 at its left end, three. And 5, bottom front right, has a block at its back and one at its left end, and holds up 4, three again. Took me longer to write that than it'll take you to do it.

And here's a check that costs nothing. Touching goes both ways. Block 1 touches block 3, so block 3's list had better have block 1 on it. If it doesn't, one of your counts is off, and now you know which two blocks to look at again. I checked fuel figures the same way for thirty years, from both ends of the column, and the one time I didn't was the one in my log that says MY MISS.
How the exam asks it. Learn the pile on its first question. Touching goes both ways, so the counts check each other.

Thirty questions in five minutes is ten seconds a question. If it runs six piles of five, the way our practice tests do, that's about fifty seconds per pile. On the old 4.5 minutes it's nine seconds, forty five a pile. The first question on a pile runs long, because that's when you're learning it. The last two go quick. That's fine. Ten seconds is a rough figure for the whole run, not a rule for each one.

Check the clock twice. At two and a half minutes you'd like to be near question fifteen, halfway. At four minutes, somewhere around twenty four. Behind? Don't hurry the counting. Hurry the deciding. Count once, pick the number, go, and don't count it again unless your number isn't among the five. If it isn't, you skipped a side or counted an edge. Run your order once more and take what you get.

With twenty seconds left and questions still open, fill every one in. Nothing comes off for a wrong answer, and Pearson wants every question answered anyway. I'd rather you guessed the last three on purpose than ran out the clock on question twenty seven with your mouth open. I timed my pallet checks my first year with a kitchen timer my mother sent me, and the timer never once made me faster. The order did. The timer just told me when I was done.
How the exam asks it. Learn the pile on the first question, then go. Answer every question before time runs out.
You had the table in January. Now I want it fast, and I want it right first.

Table Reading is ninth: 40 questions in 7 minutes on the current Pearson page, about ten and a half seconds each. The grid has X values across the top and Y values down the side, with zero in the middle of both. On our grids, and the ones I've seen, the negative values sit to the left and at the bottom. Check yours on the first question. Each question gives you an X and a Y, and you find the number where the X column and the Y row cross, then pick it out of five.

Accuracy first. Every point on this subtest is an easy point you either keep or drop. The two ways to drop one are a swapped pair and a lost sign. Swapped is when you go across to the Y number and down to the X. X minus 3, Y 5 is a different cell from X 5, Y minus 3, and the number at the swap can be sitting right there in the choices. A lost sign is when your eye finds the 4 along the top of the grid and forgets it was minus 4. I lost one over Labrador in 1976, on a temperature chart, at two in the morning, and the copilot found it before the engines did. I bought his breakfast in Goose Bay.

So say each question to yourself in the same order. X, the column. Then Y, the row. Find the column first and hold your eye on it, then come down to the row. Read the number before you look at the choices. If it's there, take it and go. If it isn't, you slipped, so start over from the labels at the edges, not from the cell you were staring at. The wrong choices are often the cells right next door, so close isn't a reason to pick one. Kit reads a feed chart at the plant that's built the same way, two labels and a cell where they meet. Her trouble there was habit, reading the new chart the way the old one ran. Read the labels every time, even on the fortieth.
How the exam asks it. Column, then row, then the cell, then the choices. A swapped pair and a lost minus sign are the two expensive misses.

Pace on Table Reading comes from rhythm. Halfway through the seven minutes, at three and a half, you want to be near question twenty. If you're behind, don't read faster. Look at the choices less. Your eye's already found the number. Match it and go. And when the clock's about to run out, put an answer on everything left.

Table Reading is a perceptual speed test. Block Counting is a spatial test on a speed clock. Both reward the same habit, accuracy first. Nobody's testing whether you can read a table or count blocks. Everybody can. They're testing whether you can do it forty times running without one slip while the clock runs, and that's why accuracy comes first. Fast and wrong is a point you had and gave back. Once you're right every time, speed comes on its own, a little each practice, the way your hands got fast on safety wire.

I flew with a copilot in 1988 who read the fuel tables so slow the aircraft commander used to hum while he waited. He was never wrong. By that fall he was the fastest on the squadron and still never wrong. I've thought about him more than I'd ever tell him.
How the exam asks it. About twenty done at three and a half minutes. Accuracy first, then pace.

Those three speed blocks come one after another, and they use three different eyes. Table Reading is lines and labels. Instrument Comprehension is a picture of the sky. Block Counting is a pile on a table. When one ends, take one breath and let it go, whatever it was. A bad table doesn't follow you into the dials unless you carry it in there.

Practice them in the order they run, at least once a week, on a clock somebody else holds. You'll learn what it feels like to switch, and the switching is half of it. I practiced star shots in the backyard one summer with a neighbor kid calling time off a stopwatch, and paid him a quarter a night.
That kid's a dentist in Joplin now. Sends Patrice a card every Christmas with a cartoon tooth on it. I tell her he owes me for the stopwatch work, and she tells me to hush.
How the exam asks it. Three clocks in a row. Let each one go when it's done, and don't carry it into the next.
The garage was cold, and the motion light came on before she had the side door all the way open.

The blue tarp was folded square on the mower seat. The crib stood in the middle of the floor, out from the wall for the first time in two years, right under the bulb. Maple, gray with garage dust, one slat cracked near the bottom. The estate sale tag still hung off a corner post. SOLD, April 2025, in grease pencil. She'd only ever seen it by one corner of tarp, in the dark. In the light it was smaller than she'd let it get in her head, and it stood out in the middle of the floor where she'd have to walk around it.

Along the top rail, clipped on with wooden clothespins from the laundry room, were seven index cards. His black marker, a question on the front of each, in square printing big enough to read from the door. A sanding block sat on the end of the rail with a sheet already wrapped around it, and under it a stack of sandpaper, eighty grit on top.
She'd asked him to teach her the seven. He hadn't said one word about the note all weekend.
Hot water on a stuck jar lid. Why does the lid come loose?
It had been number nine in his packet. She remembered guessing.
Hot water on a stuck jar lid. Why does the lid come loose?
A. The metal lid grows more than the glass when both warm up.
B. The hot water gets into the threads and greases them.
C. The heat softens the glass so the jar gives a little.
D. Heat makes things grow, so the lid gets bigger.

The metal grows more than the glass. She said it out loud to the empty garage and turned the card over. His printing again, and a lopsided jar with squiggles coming off it, the doodle he put on the board for sophomores. METAL GROWS MORE THAN GLASS. SAME HEAT, DIFFERENT STUFF. Under that, smaller: YOU GUESSED. Then she read the other six standing up, front and back, the way he read everything.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Thermal expansion. Most things grow when they warm, and different stuff grows by different amounts. A metal lid grows more than a glass jar under the same hot water, so it loosens. It's the same reason a bridge deck has gaps in it, and why power lines hang lower in August. Same heat, different stuff.
He came home at ten after four and found her out there again, in the sweatshirt she'd slept in, on an upturned bucket beside the crib with the seven cards in her lap.

Graham stood in the side door with his school bag on his shoulder. He didn't come in. He looked at the crib, then at the cards, then at her, the way he looked at a lab bench when he couldn't tell yet whether a kid had set it up right.
He looked at the crib, not at her. It's not a question. I'm not asking you for anything with it. I just got tired of it waiting in the dark for after. It can wait out here with us.
He's told her it isn't a question. What does Kit say?
A. Tell him he really didn't have to go to all this trouble.
B. Ask him to teach her the seven at the kitchen table, where it's warm.
C. Tell him she read all seven and ask which grit he starts with.
D. Tell him they'll finish it after the board, in July.

I read all seven. Which grit do you start with? Graham set his bag on the workbench. He came over, took the sanding block off the rail and turned it in his hand. Eighty. Then one twenty. Then we'll see. He put it in her hand and showed her the grain. With it, not across. Then he unclipped card two and held it up where she could see it. Convection. Go.

Right. Log it. Communication. He answered your note without a word, and you answered him the same way, plainly and right then. You didn't thank him into a corner or explain the last two years. You took what he offered and asked the next real question. The key leans toward dealing with the person in front of you, directly, at the moment it matters.

Tuesday at seven she set a quart freezer bag on Vern's yellow table, beside the percolator and the index card that still stood against it. She didn't take the picture out. He did, and held it by the edges the way you'd hold a chart somebody else had plotted.
Down the hall Patrice had the television on low, a quiz show nobody was winning. He looked at the picture until the percolator quit.
I told her that was the best seat on the airplane. I told the Lieutenant the same thing that January. I told Patrice for fifty years.
Patrice has a word for that, and she's never said it to me. Don't make it your whole personality, Sergeant. I did.
Mine was an inspection. Yours was an inspection. Mine was a seat. They were both real, Sergeant. That's why they worked so well.
He took the pencil from behind his ear, printed a word on the back of an envelope, and turned it around so she could read it. RATIONALIZE.
RATIONALIZE: closest in meaning. What does Kit tell him?
A. To think something through, carefully and sensibly.
B. To excuse something with a reason that isn't the real one.
C. To give in to something you can't change, without a fight.
D. To hand something out in fair shares, the same to each.

Talking yourself into it. A good reason standing in front of the real one. He nodded at the envelope as if it had been graded. Then he folded it once and put it in his shirt pocket, behind the pencil, and didn't take it back out.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Rationalize. To explain something away with reasons that sound good and aren't the real ones. On the test, pick the choice that says reason used as cover, not reason itself.
She went from Cedar Street straight to the plant for the eleven o'clock. Vern had handed her the week's log at the door, the way he always did. At three, on her break, she unfolded it.
Twenty four April, oh one. Night, Nebraska. Three star fix through the port. Same three stars. Same order. Every shot twice. Fix plotted in nine minutes. Best of the year. Did not hurry one of them.
Through the port. The hole in the ceiling where the stars came in. Six weeks before a girl in a green shirt sat under it and asked.

Then she went back to the pump room. Flow had come up with the weather, 1.30 million gallons a day on the meter, and Gene hadn't touched the dose since March, 2.4. Over the weekend he'd laminated a new feed chart and taped it to the wall by the pump, right over the old one she'd read at three in the morning since her first winter at the plant.
Same numbers. Gene had copied them off the new supplier's sheet, though, and the supplier ran it the other way around. Flow down the side now. Dose across the top.

Gene's new feed chart, in pounds a day. Flow in million gallons a day down the side, one point one oh up to one point four oh. Dose across the top, two point oh up to two point eight. Pounds a day where they meet.
Her hand went to the third row down and four columns over before her eyes did, the place where 2.4 and 1.30 had always met. She stopped it there.
Flow is 1.30 tonight and the dose is 2.4. What does Kit read off the chart?
A. Twenty six even, in the 1.30 row under the 2.4 column.
B. Twenty eight point two in the 1.30 row.
C. Twenty five, the same as March.
D. Twenty seven point one, third row down and four over, where it always sat.

She took her hand off the chart and read the labels first. Flow, down the side: 1.30. Dose, across the top: 2.4. Twenty six even. A pound a day more than March, which made sense with the flow up. She logged it and wrote the time beside it, and under that a note for Gene in her printing: NEW CHART RUNS FLOW DOWN THE SIDE. OLD ONE DIDN'T.

That'll hold, Sergeant. That's Table Reading at three in the morning. Read the labels before the cell, every time, and find the row by what's written on it, not by where it used to be. At the plant you've got a check: 1.30 times 2.4 times 8.34 is about 26. On the test there's no arithmetic to save you. Only the labels.

Thursday evening Graham came home with a shoebox under his arm and a look he was trying to keep off his face. Room 114, he said. Maple blocks from his density lab, every one cut the same, two inches long and an inch square. The year he'd used scrap pine, a sophomore named Dustin had argued for a week that his block was heavier on purpose.

He moved the salt and pepper and the electric bill off the kitchen table and built a little wall on the oilcloth, the way the brick runs on the library's back steps. Three along the bottom. Two riding the joints. One on top of those, like a cap.

Then masking tape and his marker. The cap got a 1, and the left one in the middle row got a 2. He put 3 on the middle of the bottom row, 4 on its left and 5 on its right, and had to do the 5 twice because the first one came out an S.
Graham's wall. Graham's wall. A pile of 6 blocks, 3 on the bottom, 2 in layer 2, 1 in layer 3. Numbered blocks: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
Did Dustin ever get his grade changed? He got a B. His mother framed it. He pushed the wall an inch toward her.

She'd gotten twenty two of thirty on his practice test, last thing before Aviation, with her eyes going. She hadn't known which ones she'd missed. He had. He'd circled all eight in red. She'd come up a block short on every one. He hadn't said so. He'd just brought the maple home.
Only faces count, the flat sides. Corners don't, edges don't, the table doesn't, and neither does my thumb. How many does two touch?
A. Three: the blocks under it and the one beside it.
C. Two: the two blocks it rests on.
D. Five: every other block in the wall.

Four. Graham said which four, and she touched them one at a time, the cap, the two under it, the one butted against its end. He lifted the cap off and set it back down, slow. The cap only covers half of it. Half a face is a face. He didn't write anything down. In Room 114 that was an A.

Right. Log it. Four. Block 1 rides on half of it, blocks 4 and 3 hold it up from underneath, and the block at its end butts against it. Half a face is a face. I lost a quarter to a loadmaster at Mather over exactly that in 1974, and he bought a Coke with it right in front of me.
Decision six. The one under it.

Saturday she'd heard the sander going in the garage half the afternoon. When she went out with two beers he showed her a knot in the top rail he swore looked like Missouri. It looked like a knot. She told him it looked just like Missouri.
On Sunday he built another one at the counter with his back to her, humming along to the oldies station, and brought it over on the cutting board like it was a birthday cake.

Eight blocks, laid the way the lumber yard stacks brick on a pallet. Four on the bottom, two by two, and four more on top the same way. From her chair she could see the four tops and the ends and sides of most of the rest. Not all of them. She leaned about an inch and he said her name.
Graham's pallet. Graham's pallet. A pile of 8 blocks, 4 on the bottom, 4 in layer 2. Numbered blocks: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
He'd stuck the 1 on the top block in the far corner, as far from her chair as it could get. Don't stand up. The test won't let you, and neither will I.
Block 1 is on top, in the far corner. How many blocks does it touch?
A. One: only the block along its side, where the seam shows.
B. Two: the block at its end and the one along its side.
C. Four: every block it can reach on top, and the one under it.
D. Three, if she counts the one underneath.

Three. Graham said show me. She pointed at the block at its end and the one along its side, then tapped the cutting board under the pile, which felt like cheating. And one under it. I can't see it. But your 1's not on the floor, so something's holding it up. Then it isn't a guess. He lifted 1 off. There it sat, plain, no number, same as the rest of them, and she felt smugger than she had all month.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Three, and one of them you never get to see. One at its end, one along its long side, and the one underneath. These piles don't float. You'd never let a jack stand take weight you couldn't account for, and it's the same arithmetic, just smaller and made of maple.
Decision seven. On her own clock.

May drill came up cold and clear. Saturday, May 1. The launch board had two two eight down for nine, and DARROW beside it in Boyd's grease pencil, same as March and April. It was the last of the three.
Fisk was at the nose at a quarter after four with two coffees. He looked rested. Whatever he'd worked out with the warehouse was holding.

Kit had Graham's sheets in her coat. Six piles of blocks he'd drawn on graph paper, five numbered blocks a pile, and a page of Table Reading he'd run off the copier in the teachers' lounge. Graham couldn't hold a clock on her at drill. She needed somebody who could, at lunch, five minutes on the dot, somebody who wouldn't say anything but time.
Fisk timed pickers on the overnight. He'd told her once that he could feel a minute go by without looking.
She wants Fisk to time her, and she's his crew chief. How does Kit ask?
A. Tell him, as his crew chief, he's running her stopwatch at lunch.
B. Ask at the morning brief if anybody'd be willing to time her at lunch.
C. Ask Boyd to put it on Fisk's list for the weekend.
D. Ask him alone at the nose as a favor that's hers, not the shop's.

Fisk. I need somebody to run a clock on me at lunch. Five minutes, and you don't say anything but time. It's mine, not the shop's. It's a favor. He looked at her over the coffee lid. I time pickers all night, Sergeant. Five minutes is nothing.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Leadership and Communication. Something you want for yourself goes to the person as an ask, in private, with the reason plain and no rank on it. You told him what it was, what it wasn't and how long it'd take. The key leans toward asking people directly and treating their time as theirs. On his own time, at lunch, and he can say no.

At eleven thirty they sat in the truck cab with the heater going and Graham's first pile sheet on her knee. Fisk set his phone on the dash, five minutes on the timer, and said go, and after that he didn't say anything.
Pile one went slow. She was learning it. Pile two went better. Somewhere in pile three Fisk said, Two thirty. That was all, which was what she'd asked for.
She was finishing question twelve. Halfway through the clock, and she'd meant to be at fifteen. Eighteen questions left, and a hundred and fifty seconds to do them in.
Eighteen to go, with two and a half minutes left. How long can Kit spend on each?
A. A bit over eight: a hundred fifty seconds over eighteen.
B. Twelve and a half: a hundred fifty over the twelve she's done.
C. Ten seconds apiece, same as the start.
D. Five: she's three behind, so cut it in half.

A hundred fifty over eighteen. Eight and a third. Not much under ten. She could do that, if she quit counting anything twice. She learned pile four on its first question and took the next four on what she knew. When Fisk said Ten seconds, she put a three on thirty without looking, and then he said time.

Right. Log it. Divide the time you've got by the questions you've got. A hundred fifty seconds over eighteen comes to eight and a third. That's not far off ten, so she isn't in trouble. She just can't afford to count anything twice. I used to run the same sum on a long track with the fuel, minutes left against receivers left, and I never liked the answer much either.

At five to three Boyd walked her as far as the stairs in the wing headquarters building and stopped there. She reads everything, Darrow. And don't be early. It annoys her. She was four minutes early. It annoyed her.

Colonel Merritt's office had a window on the ramp, a coffee ring on the blotter, and a model KC-135 on the bookcase somebody had painted the wrong gray. Kit's package lay open on the desk. The routing slip on top, five signatures. Boyd's pencil letter under that. Then her letter of intent. Merritt's finger was parked near the bottom of it, on four words.
In February I asked you why, and you told me about the wing. I'll ask once more. Why?
A. Tell her about the wing again, and say it better this time.
B. Tell her Boyd's letter says it better than she can.
C. Tell her she wants to fly for herself, in her own words.
D. Tell her eleven years on the line have earned her a shot.

Because I want to fly, ma'am. For me. I sat in the nav seat of two two eight on a family day when I was seven, and I didn't want to get out. I took this test in 2019 and missed the pilot score, and I told everybody I stayed for an inspection. I'm done telling it that way. Merritt sat back. Out the window somebody was towing a jet that wasn't two two eight. What was the number? Nineteen, ma'am. Merritt didn't write it down. It was already in the file, under her hand.

That's the fix I'd have taken. Integrity and Communication. A plain question asked twice gets a plain answer, in your own words, with the hard part in it. You didn't make it sound like a sacrifice, and you told her what's in the file before she had to find it. The key leans toward that kind of candor with the people who decide, even when it costs you.
Kit said the other thing she'd come to say, the way she'd been saying it since February. And I know about the age, ma'am. I'm five weeks over on the board date. I'd need a waiver.
It isn't a waiver, Sergeant. It's an exception to policy, and the unit sponsors it. That's me. I can put my name on it. I can't make anybody say yes.

Kit heard herself the way she'd said it to Graham in February, over the whiteboard on the kitchen table, short. There's a waiver. She'd taken Vern's long rule and cut it down to a word that wasn't even the right word.

My name on it is necessary. It isn't enough. The yes comes from above this wing, from people I don't get to call, and when they read it they'll be reading my judgment as much as your number. Some of them remember the last one.

She turned the package face down. Two years ago I sent Sergeant Haas to pilot training on heart. Everybody liked him. I liked him. He washed out, the wing lost the slot, and he came home to the shop. I ask him first, every time I tell it. He's always said tell them. So I tell them.
I'll endorse your exception if your number lets me. Not before. So what do you want from me, Sergeant?
A. Nothing, ma'am, only a fair look at the number.
B. Mention that Vern Pruett flew with her and teaches her now.
C. Her endorsement, if the number earns it.
D. Ask her to call above the wing herself and push for it.

Your name on the exception to policy, ma'am, if the number earns it. I'll bring you the number. Merritt looked at her a long moment. Then she turned the package face up again and squared it to the edge of the desk. That I can do. Scores post the eighteenth? Kit said they did. Tuesday.

That'll hold, Sergeant. Communication. You asked for exactly what's hers to give, in plain words, and you took her condition without arguing it. A direct ask inside someone's limits is about the strongest ask there is. And you put the work where it belongs, on you.

Sunday, May 2, at release, she went the long way out, past avionics. Corbin was at the far bench with a fuel gauge open in front of him and a magnifier on a gooseneck. He didn't look up. She told you. Kit said she had. Why do you let her? Corbin turned the gauge over. Because she asks.

Friday night, May 7, she was in the garage at twenty to twelve with the fourth sheet of Graham's second set, and she'd been at it since nine. The crib was down to bare wood on three sides. The seven cards from April still hung on the rail, soft at the corners from handling, and Graham had clipped new ones beside them as she learned the old: three Table Reading cards, two with block piles drawn small.
Practice Test 2 was at eight in the morning at the kitchen table, all eleven blocks. A week after that, the real one.
Graham came out in his socks with a dish towel over his shoulder. He didn't say anything about the time. He looked at the clock over the workbench, and so did she.
It's twenty to twelve, and the practice test starts at eight. What does Kit do?
A. Finish this sheet and run one more Table Reading page, then sleep.
B. Skip tomorrow's practice test and keep drilling the speed blocks.
C. Stay out here and run every speed block twice, since it's the last night.
D. Stop now and go to bed.

I'm done. She clipped the pile sheet to the rail with the cards, brushed the dust off the bucket, and set two pencils on the kitchen table beside Graham's packets. She was asleep before twelve. If she dreamed about blocks, she didn't count them.

Right. Log it. Resource management, and the resource is you. The night before a five hour test, sleep buys more points than one more pile. You set a stopping point and kept it, and got ready for the morning instead of the last question. On the test the key leans toward the action that plans the time and looks after the people doing the work.

Saturday, May 8, eight o'clock, the kitchen table again. Graham ran the clock the way he had in April. He said one word at the end of each block. The rest of the time he graded lab reports in red across from her and never looked up.
She'd slept, and by Table Reading she could feel it, her eye going to the labels first without being told.

Instrument Comprehension, five minutes, and she only froze once. Then Block Counting. Pile four in Graham's packet was three blocks lying crossways on the table and two more lying long across those, front and back. One stood on end over on the right like a chimney, and one more lay crossways on top.
Graham's packet, pile four. Graham's packet, pile four. A pile of 7 blocks, 3 on the bottom, 3 in layer 2, 1 in layer 3. Numbered blocks: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

Blocks 1 and 2 on this pile were already behind her, so she knew how it went together. Across the table Graham flipped a lab report over, read the back, and made the face he made at bad handwriting. Two houses down the neighbors' beagle had found something to bark at. Block 4 sat in the middle of the bottom row. She'd about used up her fifty seconds on this pile.
Block 4, on a pile she's already worked twice. How many blocks does it touch?
A. Five: block 2 where it meets it, plus both sides and the two on top.
B. Four: a block on each side and two lying long across its top.
C. Two: just the two lying across its top.
D. Three: block 5 beside it and the two lying across its top.

She'd met block 3 and the plain one behind it on block 1, so the top was done before she looked. Plain block on the left, 5 on the right, and that made four. She marked it. Graham's red pen kept scratching, and she went on to 5, which she already knew touched 4.

That's the fix I'd have taken. It's four. Block 3 and the plain one behind it lie long across its top. You only get a strip of the back one. A plain block on its left, block 5 on its right, and block 2 next door gets nothing but an edge. A pile you've worked once hands you half the next answer. That's about the only free thing in the building that day, and the coffee isn't.
Graham marked the packets at the table while she mowed the side yard, which needed it this time.

The cover page went on the fridge under the whiteboard magnet. Table Reading, thirty eight of forty. Block Counting, twenty seven of thirty. Physical Science, seventeen of twenty, and beside that one, in red, a little jar with wavy heat lines coming off it.

The whiteboard ran out tomorrow. Sunday, May 9, was the last square he'd drawn in February. MAY 15 sat down in the corner with no question mark, and past the last column the board was white to its aluminum edge, the way it had always been. Neither of them reached for a marker.
After supper she went out to the garage by herself. Three sides were bare maple now, pale as a new ball bat. The jar card on the rail had a sawdust thumbprint on it, probably hers.

She picked up the sanding block and went at the last rail. Graham came out with the red pen still in his hand, set it on the mower seat beside a can of stain he'd bought Thursday and hadn't mentioned, and stood behind her.
Easy. You're pushing. You've said that every night since April.

He put his hand over hers on the block. Down the rail and back, slower, and he let her steer. His phone went off on the workbench, some parent, and he let it go. Nobody said July, or any month after it.
